title: Interest rates come down
trigger: A central bank cuts its rates to stimulate the economy.
mechanism: Money becomes cheaper to borrow. Companies invest more readily, and risk-free savings pay less — which makes shares relatively more attractive.
portfolio: Growth stocks, which live off future investment, usually react the most. Banks, on the other hand, see their lending margins squeezed.
lesson: A rate cut is not good news for everyone at once. The sector decides.

title: Inflation picks up again
trigger: Prices rise faster than expected for several months.
mechanism: Every euro buys less than before. Central banks often raise rates to slow the rise, which makes credit more expensive.
portfolio: Companies able to raise their prices without losing customers — luxury, certain brands — absorb the shock better than those stuck with rising costs.
lesson: The real return on an investment is what it earns once inflation is deducted.

title: The economy enters a recession
trigger: Activity contracts for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Households and companies spend less. Profits fall, and markets price that fall in before it shows up in the accounts.
portfolio: So-called defensive sectors — healthcare, food, industrial gases — usually fall less than cyclical ones such as carmakers or luxury.
lesson: Recessions are part of the cycle. Historically markets have come through them — but never on a predictable schedule.

title: Tech keeps pulling the indices along
trigger: A handful of very large technology companies accounts for most of the rise in the indices.
mechanism: When a few stocks weigh heavily in an index, the index's performance mostly reflects theirs — even if the hundreds of other companies are flat.
portfolio: A portfolio that looks diversified can in fact run on the same engine as the index, if its main holdings belong to the same sector.
lesson: Diversifying is not about multiplying holdings: it is about multiplying engines.
